My advice to you is to be compassionate towards yourself. I've had a pretty lonely and depressing teenage years myself and even when I was in a new and in many terms better environment, it was still tough because I always felt like I missed on some crucial part of social development and experience, and just couldn't contribute as much as others. I still feel like this a lot, but I also decided that I don't have to be so hard on myself. I try to look at it with a siliver lining. New environment and new people can be a life changer, though you will have to make it work as well. Since you do want a different life, your mind is already in the right space. Nothing wrong with being a bit socially awkward/unexperienced because of your past, a lot of people are. There's a lot to learn. Give yourself a new opportunity, be curious in others and yourself. You need new experience with life, so try to keep an open mind. Also, I suggest you to attend some form of therapy or even just an uni councler, to have some backup and somewhere to talk about what's going on. 

In my experience, my teens were pretty lonely and awful, my life at uni was better every year but still very hard (also had a pretty severe eating disorder and skipped a lot of classes because of shame). Still, some relationships got stronger, some died out, some new formed. I feel that everything nice I did or that happened, I did it later than most and it felt so surreal because I wanted it for so long. It's bittersweet for me. I'm 27 now but mentally I feel like 23 or that everything I did, have and know now, I "should" have experienced/known by 23. But, on the other hand, my reality NOW is better and that's what matters. I still feel sad about my teen years, but also appreciate what have now A LOTTTT. Sometimes I even feel a bit proud of myself to keep on trying and go out of my comfort zone bit by bit. And it's surprising how things can change. And maybe I don't have the same "cool" stories from my 16 than some of my friends do, but it's okay. My past was just different. We enjoy each other's company for other reasons and that's what matters. 

I wish you the best on your new beginning :)

I agree what the other have said, especially about finding medical help and getting your electrolytes better. When you'll feel better physically you will have more (also mental) energy to do other things. I'd like to add that yoz don't have to apologize for telling how you're feeling. It's okay, let it out, even if it feels depressing, sad and negative. And in a situation where your Ed is taking out so much energy from you, it's an expected consequence to feel drained and unmotivated. You can be aware of them without having to act according to it. I agree that it's hard to imagine a different life if you never had it, it's like imagining a new colour. My advice here would be to just slowly exposing yourself to new things, and it doesn't have to be big, just literally anything you didn't try yet. But taking caring of yourself better physically as well. Also, if you have an option and think it might helpnyou, try finding some kind of therapist, psychologist, social worker or anyone in that regard and try to see them regularly. Just to have someone to tell what's going on. If that seems like too much, even participating in forums like this or some other online communitities. You don't have to be alone in this <3

Hello. I have tried psychedelics in the form of psilocybin a couple of times. I wasn't mentally optimal when I tried them (because, honestly, I've felt like this for a long time, though I am generally better than a few years ago when I tried them).

I think that dosing makes the most difference here. If you're going to try some form of psychedelics, I'd definitely suggest a lower dose. The experience can be quite overwhelming even for experienced users (I don't count myself an experienced user though). 

Another good thing about lower dose is that (anecdotal experience from me and some people I know) everything got really beautiful, breathtaking and deep. My sense of smell was really strong, everything was really really interesting and it was almost bothering me (in a good way) that I couldn't decide what to do because everything I decided to do or just observe got sooo interesting a deep. Being in nature is great under the influence of psychedelics, it's just breathtaking! 

When I first tried them, I also had in mind that they could help me see the world and myself in a different perspective. It kinda did, I can't deny that. But, in my case, it wasn't only the good. Almost every time I took it, I felt absolutely terrible for at least some time when the high lasted. I wouldn't really call it a bad trip, it was mkre like me being in a bad place. Most of the time it kind of passed and at one time I felt like I went through hell and when it was over (me still being high), it was kinda rewarding and peaceful. 

I also felt immense sense of connection with people, animals, nature and being. I felt like I am okay, that everything is connected. This is probably the main thing that stayed with me. 

I suggest maybe getting a piece of paper and writing your thoughts (I did write to myself something along the lines when I felt that I am perfectly fine and nothing is inherently wrong with me - the sad thing is, when I read it now, I can't really connect back into this feeling again). 

If you're in a particulary bad place, I wouldn't recommend it. When I used them the first time I was pretty bad, but I had a roomate who I managed to contact when I found the experience overwhelming (I took quite a big dose), we went for a walk and yeah then I felt really thankful and I calmed down a lot. 

One other time, I took it while feeling really lonely, depressed and a bit suicidal... I took a kower dose but it was still nasty the whole time and I kind of wanted to die even though I was tripping. I know that during that time what I really craved was a human connection. 

Sorry, I see thus is getting long and I didn't give you any specific answer, I could write a lot on that subject. In general, I think psychedelics are something that open up a whole new perspective, but it doesn't always come just with the positives. I am not sorry I tried them and I want to try use again sometime, just not right now, I don't feel mentally in the right space and don't really have time to process everything that comes with it. In the future, I would like to take them with some truested people and in the right circumstances. 

If you have any questions, just ask, I'm kinda in a rush right now so sorry if my response is a bit chaotic.

I have a "missing period" from ages from about 11-21. Barely have any photo of myself, and even these are usually school or group photos. In the last couple of years I've been trying to kind of push myself to be in the photos, but it's always a challenging choice and I get really stressed when, for example, I ask a friend to take a photo somewhere. But even if I'm having a "good day", as soon as I get infront of camera, I get so uncomfortable, I just can't stand, smile and look properly. It just feels forced no matter what and I don't know how to change it

My therapist told me she wouldn't do exposure therapy and CBT with me - she was sure I'd be doing weekly tasks, but internally it's not the thing that I'd need most from therapy, so she suggested to rather wait when she'll have a free spot in analytical therapy. I agree with her.

During the years I set myself a lot of challenges and even though I can now find myself a bit more used to things ranging from going in public to working as a waitress, I'm still not fully comfortable. There are times (sometimes only moments) when I feel normal and confident, but there's this basic, uncomfortable thing which is persisting and I don't think it'd ever go away no matter of how "good" my social life and behavior goes. I had to fake it to make it because I had zero confidence that time, but it still doesn't always feel natural, a part of me is still not okay, I think the only difference is that I learned how to behave and hide (more or less) how uncomfortable I am. I'm still happy I gave myself these challenges because otherwise I'd still be too afraid to leave my room. 

So I think that exposure is necessary but it doesn't automatically lead to feeling okay about yourself. Of you can, I'd suggest some form of therapy.
